The point is this: before a thing exists, God’s knowledge of it is knowledge of what will exist. Once the thing actually exists, however, knowledge that it “will exist” would no longer match reality, because the thing can no longer correctly be described as something that will exist. Correct knowledge would now have to be knowledge that it has come into existence. So once the thing has been created, the original object of the first knowledge has disappeared. That knowledge should therefore disappear too and be replaced by new knowledge whose object is the thing that “has come into existence,” not the thing that “will come into existence.” If the first knowledge remained unchanged, it would no longer match reality and would therefore amount to ignorance.↩︎
In other words, if the first knowledge—knowledge of “what will exist”—changes into knowledge of “what has come into existence,” then God’s knowledge has changed.↩︎

The argument is that if God’s knowledge changes, then it has undergone something that happens to every created, non-eternal thing: change. Since what is eternal does not change, God’s knowledge would therefore have to be non-eternal.↩︎

The point is that if God’s knowledge comes into existence within God’s own being, two problems follow. First, God’s being itself would have changed: it was previously without this knowledge and then became the bearer of it once the knowledge arose. But God’s being is eternal, and what is eternal cannot change. Second, this would make God’s being a place in which new events occur. That too is impossible, because anything that serves as a place for events is spatially limited, whereas God is not limited by space.↩︎
In other words, since God’s knowledge cannot be said to arise within God’s own being for the two reasons just given, it must arise in some locus other than God’s being.↩︎

That is, if we say God’s knowledge arises in some locus, then that locus becomes characterized by this knowledge: the knowledge becomes an attribute of the locus in which it arose. We would then have to call that locus “knowing,” even though it is God who is “the Knower.”↩︎

Since, as the argument has shown, God’s knowledge cannot arise either within God’s own being or in some particular locus outside it, we are left with one unavoidable conclusion: God’s knowledge has no locus.↩︎
